figures.name: John Chrysostom
also_known_as: Chrysostomos ("Golden-mouthed", a title given after his death)
figures.places: Antioch in Syria (born, schooled, monk in the nearby mountains, deacon 381, priest 386); Constantinople (archbishop from 398); exiled 403 and again 404 to Cucusus in Armenia; died at Comana in Pontus on the road to a harsher exile
figures.role: Preacher of Antioch and archbishop of Constantinople; the most famous preacher of the Greek Church
figures.status_note: Saint in the Orthodox, Catholic and Oriental churches and commemorated by Anglicans and Lutherans; Doctor of the Church (Catholic); one of the Three Holy Hierarchs (Orthodox); the usual Orthodox Sunday liturgy bears his name. Deposed in his lifetime by the Synod of the Oak (403), led by Theophilus of Alexandria, and exiled by the court; rehabilitated after his death. Caution for readers: his eight sermons Against the Jews (Antioch, 386-387) are violent invective against Jews and against Christians who kept Jewish feasts, and were later used by antisemites. Anyone quoting him should know this.
figures.hook: He told the rich of Constantinople that keeping their surplus from the poor was robbery; the empress had him exiled twice, and he died on the road saying "Glory to God for all things."

stories.story: His widowed mother sat him on the bed where she had given birth to him and begged him, in tears, not to leave home for the monastic life with his friend Basil: "do not plunge me into a second widowhood" and "wait for my death". He stayed.

When he and his friend Basil heard they were about to be made bishops, he promised to go along with whatever Basil did, then hid. Basil was seized and ordained, told that John had yielded meekly. John then defended the trick at length as a good kind of deceit. He mentions in passing that he was the one people thought 'the more hot tempered'.

As a young man he lived four years with an old hermit in the mountains near Antioch, then two years alone in a cave, hardly sleeping and never lying down. It wrecked his stomach and kidneys, and he had to come back to the city, which his biographer calls providence for the Church.
stories.source: Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom, chapter 5 (tr. H. Moore, 1921)

stories.story: As archbishop he audited the church accounts, cut the bishop's own lavish spending, sent the money to the hospital, and built more hospitals with doctors and cooks so that strangers who fell ill in the city could be cared for.

He refused to give or attend dinner parties and ate alone, which his enemies called arrogance. His friend Palladius defended the habit: the bishop had to invite everyone or no one, and dinners wasted money the poor needed.

When a silver statue of the Empress Eudoxia was set up beside the cathedral with noisy games around it, he mocked those responsible from the pulpit. The historian Socrates says he then opened a sermon with 'Again Herodias raves; again she is troubled; she dances again; and again desires to receive John's head in a charger.' He was exiled for the second time.

Epiphanius of Cyprus came to Constantinople and acted against him. Socrates reports, while saying he cannot vouch for it, that Epiphanius said on leaving, 'I hope that you will not die a bishop', and John answered, 'Expect not to arrive at your own country.' Epiphanius died at sea; John was deposed.

Hearing that pagan worship still flourished in Phoenicia, he sent zealous monks armed with imperial edicts to pull down the temples, and paid the demolition crews with gifts from wealthy Christian women rather than public money. In the same years he gave the Gothic Christians in the capital a church of their own with services in their language.
Dying on a forced march into deeper exile, he asked for white clothes, gave away everything else he had, received Communion and prayed his usual words, 'Glory to God for all things', before he died.

temperament.evidence: Telling the story of his own ordination escape, he says the bystanders called him the one 'generally reputed to be the more hot tempered (meaning me)'.

temperament.trait: Stern, outspoken, thought haughty in private
temperament.evidence: Socrates: 'on account of his zeal for temperance he was stern and severe'; an early friend said 'that in his youth he manifested a proneness to irritability, rather than to modesty'; 'the liberty of speech he allowed himself was offensive to very many'; 'in private conversation he was frequently thought haughty and assuming by those who did not know him.'

temperament.trait: Would not stop preaching an unwelcome message
temperament.evidence: After telling the rich to free their slaves: 'And I know that I am giving disgust to my hearers. But what must I do? For this I am set, and I shall not cease to say these things, whether anything comes of them or not.'
Palladius admits 'he used to eat alone' and defends it against charges of pride.

temperament.trait: Tender and steady as a friend in trouble
temperament.evidence: From exile he wrote long letters to the deaconess Olympias to lift her despondency, asking her to tell him honestly how she was: 'pray do not deceive me by saying that you have thrown off all despondency'.

genuine_lines.quote: Would you do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked; do not while here you honor Him with silken garments, neglect Him perishing without of cold and nakedness.
genuine_lines.translation: G. Prevost, rev. M. B. Riddle, NPNF 1st series vol. 10 (1888), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: remember constantly that not to share our own riches with the poor is a robbery of the poor, and a depriving them of their livelihood; and that that which we possess is not only our own, but also theirs.
genuine_lines.work: On the Rich Man and Lazarus, Discourse 2
genuine_lines.translation: F. Allen, Four Discourses of Chrysostom (London, 1869)

genuine_lines.quote: Mercy is called by that name for this reason, that it gives even to the unworthy.
genuine_lines.work: On the Rich Man and Lazarus, Discourse 2
genuine_lines.translation: F. Allen, Four Discourses of Chrysostom (London, 1869)

genuine_lines.quote: Tempers are wanted, not talking; character, not cleverness; deeds, not words.
genuine_lines.translation: G. Alexander, NPNF 1st series vol. 13 (1889), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For there is only one thing, Olympias, which is really terrible, only one real trial, and that is sin
genuine_lines.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF 1st series vol. 9 (1889), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For it is not God that grants to play, but the devil.
genuine_lines.translation: G. Prevost, rev. M. B. Riddle, NPNF 1st series vol. 10 (1888), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: I do not think there are many among Bishops that will be saved, but many more that perish
genuine_lines.translation: J. Walker, J. Sheppard and H. Browne, NPNF 1st series vol. 11 (1889), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Glory to God for all things
genuine_lines.work: His customary prayer and last words, recorded by Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom
genuine_lines.translation: H. Moore (London: SPCK, 1921)

misattributed.line: He who is not angry when he has cause, sins.
misattributed.truth: From the Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum (Homily 11), an anonymous fifth-century Arian commentary long printed among Chrysostom's works and quoted as his by Aquinas. Not Chrysostom.

misattributed.line: If you cannot find Christ in the beggar at the church door, you will not find Him in the chalice.
misattributed.truth: A modern paraphrase circulating online, not a line in his works. The real passage is Homily 50 on Matthew: 'Would you do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked...'

misattributed.line: The road (or floor) of hell is paved with the skulls of priests (or bishops).
misattributed.truth: No confirmed source in his works. The genuine line is milder: 'I do not think there are many among Bishops that will be saved, but many more that perish' (Homily 3 on Acts).

misattributed.line: Again Herodias raves; again she is troubled; she dances again; and again desires to receive John's head in a charger.
misattributed.truth: Known only because the historians Socrates (6.18) and Sozomen report it as the opening of a sermon against Eudoxia. The sermon that survives with these words is judged spurious. Quote it as 'reported by Socrates', not as his text.

opinions.position: Keeping your wealth from the poor is not just stingy; it is robbery. What you own belongs to them too.
opinions.side_note: The strongest 'wealth' side: private surplus is owed to the poor.
opinions.quote: remember constantly that not to share our own riches with the poor is a robbery of the poor, and a depriving them of their livelihood; and that that which we possess is not only our own, but also theirs.
opinions.work: On the Rich Man and Lazarus, Discourse 2
opinions.translation: F. Allen, Four Discourses of Chrysostom (London, 1869)
opinions.today: Sharply split. Many people, religious or not, feel the rich owe the poor something, but most would call not giving 'selfish', not 'theft'. The word robbery is the test; it divides readers well.

opinions.topic: new: give without checking if they deserve it
opinions.position: When someone is in need, give. Do not ask about their past or whether they deserve it; need is their only claim.
opinions.side_note: Against means-testing charity.
opinions.quote: It becomes him that is truly well-disposed not to require an account of a man's past life, but simply to relieve poverty and to satisfy want.
opinions.work: On the Rich Man and Lazarus, Discourse 2
opinions.translation: F. Allen, Four Discourses of Chrysostom (London, 1869)
opinions.today: Genuinely split. Plenty of people won't give cash to a beggar who might misuse it, and many charities vet recipients; others give to anyone who asks. A good everyday statement.

opinions.topic: new: beautiful churches or the poor
opinions.position: Gold cups and silk hangings mean nothing to Christ if His poor are left cold outside. Help the poor first; the poor man is more truly a temple than the building.
opinions.side_note: He adds that he is not forbidding gifts to the church, only putting the poor first.
opinions.quote: Do not therefore while adorning His house overlook your brother in distress, for he is more properly a temple than the other.
opinions.translation: G. Prevost, rev. M. B. Riddle, NPNF 1st series vol. 10 (1888), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split, and a live argument: money for a new church roof, an organ or a cathedral versus money for the hungry. Many Catholics and Orthodox defend beauty in worship; many others side with Chrysostom.

opinions.topic: new: can anyone get rich honestly
opinions.position: Great fortunes are almost never innocent. If you trace any large inheritance back far enough, you find someone who took what was not theirs, because God made the earth for all alike.
opinions.side_note: He softens it at once: 'you are not responsible for the covetous acts of your father'.
opinions.quote: So destructive a passion is avarice, that to grow rich without injustice is impossible.
opinions.translation: P. Schaff (ed.), NPNF 1st series vol. 13 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split, along political lines more than religious ones. Some say every fortune has a crime behind it; others say most wealth is earned by work and risk.

opinions.position: If the Christians of a city pooled their property the way the first church in Jerusalem did, no one would go hungry; living separately is what makes people poor.
opinions.side_note: He presents it as a thought experiment ('in words, I mean') while plainly wishing it.
opinions.quote: For so it is, division always makes diminution, concord and agreement make increase. The dwellers in the monasteries live just as the faithful did then: now did ever any of these die of hunger?
opinions.translation: J. Walker, J. Sheppard and H. Browne, NPNF 1st series vol. 11 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would reject pooling all property; a minority (intentional communities, some religious orders, socialists) would cheer. One-sided but with a passionate minority.

opinions.position: Keeping crowds of servants is vanity. If you must buy slaves, teach them a trade so they can support themselves and set them free.
opinions.side_note: He did not demand abolition: he would 'allow you to keep a second servant'.
opinions.quote: when you have purchased them and have taught them trades whereby to support themselves, let them go free.
opinions.translation: T. W. Chambers, NPNF 1st series vol. 12 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: One-sided today: everyone condemns slavery, so this cannot be a quiz statement as it stands. His underlying point (paying others to serve you is mostly pride; do things for yourself) could be recast and would split people.

opinions.position: Deceiving someone for their own good is not a sin; it is good management, like a doctor's trick to get a patient to take medicine.
opinions.side_note: The permissive side of the lying claim. Written to justify his own trick on his friend Basil. Augustine held the opposite: never lie.
opinions.quote: For great is the value of deceit, provided it be not introduced with a mischievous intention. In fact action of this kind ought not to be called deceit, but rather a kind of good management, cleverness and skill
opinions.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF 1st series vol. 9 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Most people tell white lies and think a kind deception can be right; a strict minority say lying is always wrong. A strong statement.

opinions.position: Being a church leader is so dangerous to the soul that he fled it himself and thought most bishops would be damned.
opinions.side_note: The 'fear office' side. His own life matches: he hid to avoid being made a bishop as a young man.
opinions.quote: I do not think there are many among Bishops that will be saved, but many more that perish: and the reason is, that it is an affair that requires a great mind.
opinions.translation: J. Walker, J. Sheppard and H. Browne, NPNF 1st series vol. 11 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split between people who think power corrupts and should be avoided and people who think good people have a duty to lead.

opinions.position: Christians should not live for fun and laughter. Christ is recorded weeping but never laughing; the wish to 'laugh and play all my days' is childish.
opinions.side_note: The austere side. He adds that he does not mean 'to suppress all laughter, but to take away dissipation of mind'.
opinions.quote: Nay, far be it from me to weep at any time, but may God grant me to laugh and to play all my days. And what can be more childish than this mind? For it is not God that grants to play, but the devil.
opinions.translation: G. Prevost, rev. M. B. Riddle, NPNF 1st series vol. 10 (1888), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Mostly one-sided against him: nearly everyone today thinks fun and laughter are good and healthy. A useful 'sparring partner' statement because few agree.

opinions.position: The theatre is the devil's workshop. Do not tell me it is only acting: acting has made many adulterers and broken many homes.
opinions.side_note: The strict side of the shows claim.
opinions.quote: Nay, tell me not, that what is done is acting; for this acting has made many adulterers, and subverted many families.
opinions.translation: G. Prevost, rev. M. B. Riddle, NPNF 1st series vol. 10 (1888), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split in its modern form: 'watching sex on screen changes how people behave' versus 'it is just entertainment'.

opinions.topic: new: ordinary people and the Bible
opinions.position: Reading the Bible is not just for monks and clergy. People with jobs, spouses and children need it more, because they take more wounds every day.
opinions.quote: Why, this is what has ruined all, your supposing that the reading of the divine Scriptures appertains to those only, when you need it much more than they. For they that dwell in the world, and each day receive wounds, these have most need of medicines.
opinions.translation: G. Prevost, rev. M. B. Riddle, NPNF 1st series vol. 10 (1888), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Among Christians today nearly everyone agrees in principle, so weak as a statement; but 'busy people need spiritual reading more than retreat-goers do' would divide people.

opinions.position: The monk has it easy: he is in a calm harbour. The person living in the world is out at sea in the storm, and needs spiritual help more.
opinions.side_note: Change of life: as a young man he went to live as a hermit in a cave and ruined his health (Palladius, chapter 5); as a preacher he told city people their life was the harder one. He never stopped admiring monks.
opinions.quote: The one is entered as it were into a waveless harbor, and lives an untroubled life, and far removed from every storm; while the other is ever on the ocean
opinions.translation: G. Alexander, NPNF 1st series vol. 13 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some people think withdrawing from the world is the harder, holier path; others think staying in the mess of work and family is the real test.

opinions.position: Do not bring your son up to be a clever speaker; bring him up to be good. Character matters, cleverness does not.
opinions.side_note: He studied rhetoric under the famous pagan Libanius, so this is a trained orator rating eloquence low. He allows ordinary schooling 'to prevent your attending to them exclusively'.
opinions.quote: study not to make him an orator, but train him up to be a philosopher. In the want of the one there will be no harm whatever; in the absence of the other, all the rhetoric in the world will be of no advantage.
opinions.translation: G. Alexander, NPNF 1st series vol. 13 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split in its modern form: 'I would rather my child be good than successful' is popular to say, but parents' real choices (grades, universities, careers) often show the opposite.

opinions.position: A husband's love must go as far as Christ's: he should be ready to die for his wife, and win her by care, never by threats or force.
opinions.side_note: He also teaches the wife's obedience; the demand he lays on the husband is the striking half.
opinions.quote: Yea, even if it shall be needful for you to give your life for her, yea, and to be cut into pieces ten thousand times, yea, and to endure and undergo any suffering whatever — refuse it not.
opinions.translation: G. Alexander, NPNF 1st series vol. 13 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Few would disagree with self-giving love; the 'head and obedience' frame around it divides people sharply.

opinions.position: Husband and wife should never say 'mine' about money. They are one person; separate property is the devil's word.
opinions.quote: You both have become one man, one living creature; and do you still say my own? Cursed and abominable word that it is, it was brought in by the devil.
opinions.translation: G. Alexander, NPNF 1st series vol. 13 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Genuinely split today: joint accounts versus separate finances is a real and common disagreement between couples. Excellent everyday statement.

opinions.position: Do not choose or praise a spouse for beauty. Its thrill lasts a month or a year, then fades; look for beauty of soul.
opinions.quote: Praise her not for her beauty. Praise and hatred and love based on personal beauty belong to unchastened souls. Seek thou for beauty of soul.
opinions.translation: G. Alexander, NPNF 1st series vol. 13 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split in practice: people say character matters most, but many also say attraction is essential. 'Attraction matters a lot in choosing a partner' would divide a room.

opinions.position: Parents let their children learn every popular song but not a single psalm. Homes should sing psalms instead of the songs of the street and stage.
opinions.side_note: The strict side on secular music.
opinions.quote: But now your children will utter songs and dances of Satan, like cooks, and caterers, and musicians; no one knows any psalm, but it seems a thing to be ashamed of even, and a mockery, and a joke.
opinions.translation: J. Ashworth, rev. G. Alexander, NPNF 1st series vol. 13 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Mostly against him today; a minority of Christian families limit secular music. Works as a sparring statement.

opinions.position: Weep for your dead; it is natural and Christ wept too. But grieve gently, not with wailing, tearing hair and beating yourself, as if there were no resurrection.
opinions.side_note: The moderate side: grief allowed, excess forbidden.
opinions.quote: No, neither do I forbid weeping, but I forbid the beating yourselves, the weeping immoderately. I am neither brutal nor cruel. I know that our nature asks and seeks for its friends and daily companions; it cannot but be grieved.
opinions.translation: C. Marriott, rev. P. Schaff, NPNF 1st series vol. 14 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split on the edges: many today say there is no wrong way to grieve and loud grief is healthy; others value composure. The 'is there a wrong way to grieve?' form would divide people.

opinions.position: No fall is too far for God to lift you back up, even higher than before. What sinks people is not how much they have sinned but giving up hope.
opinions.side_note: Written to a friend, Theodore, who had left the monastic life. The generous side of second chances.
opinions.quote: Do not then despair of the most perfect change. For if the devil had such great power as to cast you down from that pinnacle and height of virtue into the extremity of evil doing, much more will God be able to draw you up again to your former confidence
opinions.work: An Exhortation to Theodore after His Fall, Letter 1
opinions.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF 1st series vol. 9 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree in principle, so weak alone; it becomes a real split when asked about specific people (a pastor who fell, a friend who betrayed you).

opinions.position: Someone who holds a grudge and keeps an enemy should not come to Communion, any more than an adulterer. Be reconciled first, and quickly.
opinions.quote: For as it is not to be imagined that the fornicator and the blasphemer can partake of the sacred Table, so it is impossible that he who has an enemy, and bears malice, can enjoy the holy Communion.
opinions.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF 1st series vol. 9 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split, in a softer form: 'a grudge is as serious as a sexual sin' would surprise many, who treat resentment as understandable and sex as the bigger matter.

opinions.position: Do not swear oaths, and do not make others swear, not even in court or on the Gospels. Christ said 'swear not at all'. If you trust a man, you do not need his oath; if he is a liar, you only push him into perjury.
opinions.side_note: He campaigned against oaths through a whole Lent in Antioch (387).
opinions.quote: If you believe that the man is true, do not impose the obligation of the oath; but if you know him to be a liar, do not force him to commit perjury.
opinions.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF 1st series vol. 9 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: One-sided today: almost everyone accepts oaths in court and at weddings; only Quakers, Mennonites and some others refuse. A sparring statement.

opinions.topic: new: the only thing worth fearing
opinions.position: Nothing is truly terrible except sin. Exile, slander, losing your property, even the sword are not real evils.
opinions.side_note: Written from exile to a grieving friend; he practised it.
opinions.quote: For there is only one thing, Olympias, which is really terrible, only one real trial, and that is sin
opinions.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF 1st series vol. 9 (1889), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many people, including many Christians, think suffering, loss and injustice are real evils in their own right, not only sin.

opinions.position: He used imperial edicts and bands of monks to tear down the remaining pagan temples in Phoenicia.
opinions.side_note: Evidence is an act reported by the historian Theodoret (c. 450), not Chrysostom's own words. It puts him on the side of using state power against paganism.
opinions.quote: John got together certain monks who were fired with divine zeal, armed them with imperial edicts and dispatched them against the idols' shrines.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 3 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost no one today supports destroying other religions' places of worship, so as a statement it is one-sided; the question behind it (should the law favour Christianity?) still splits people.

sparring.over: Theophilus resented Chrysostom's shelter of the Egyptian 'Tall Brothers' monks and led the Synod of the Oak (403), which deposed him. Palladius's Dialogue is a sustained defence against Theophilus.
sparring.source: Palladius, Dialogue, chapters 1-11; Socrates, Ecclesiastical History 6.15

sparring.over: Origen and the Tall Brothers; Epiphanius ordained a deacon in Chrysostom's city without leave, and they parted with an exchange of barbed prophecies (reported with Socrates's own doubts).
His sermons against luxury and against the games at her silver statue; she took his words personally and pressed for his deposition and exile.
A visiting Syrian bishop and preacher left in charge while Chrysostom was away; a feud followed and Severian joined his enemies.

sparring.with: His own clergy and the bishops of Asia
sparring.over: He disciplined the Constantinople clergy harshly and deposed Asian bishops for buying their offices; many became his enemies.

John Chrysostom, Deesis tier of the Trinity Cathedral, Trinity-Sergius Lavra

figures.name: John Cassian
figures.places: Probably born in Scythia Minor (the Dobruja, modern Romania; disputed, some say Gaul); monk in Bethlehem; about fifteen years among the monks of Egypt (Scetis and the Nile delta); Constantinople (made deacon by John Chrysostom); Rome (404-405, carrying the Constantinople clergy's appeal for Chrysostom); Marseille from about 415, where he founded a monastery for men and one for women
figures.role: Monk, abbot and writer who carried the teaching of the Egyptian desert to the Latin West
figures.status_note: Saint in the Orthodox Church (feast 29 February, kept on 28 February in other years). In the West never formally canonized, but venerated at Marseille (feast 23 July) and treated as a saint by Gregory the Great. Benedict's Rule tells monks to read his Conferences and Institutes. Caution: his Conference 13 says the first movement of a good will can sometimes come from ourselves; Prosper of Aquitaine attacked it (without naming him) about 433, and later centuries called the view 'Semipelagian' (a much later label). The Council of Orange (529) rejected that view. He himself condemned Pelagius.
figures.hook: After years among the holiest monks of Egypt, he admitted that alone in his cell he still lost his temper, at his pen for being too thick, at his knife for being blunt, and at his flint when it would not spark.

stories.story: Living as a hermit, he found he was angry at his pen, his penknife and his flint, and could calm down only by cursing them or the devil. His lesson: going off alone does not cure a bad temper; it only takes away the people you blame.

He and his lifelong friend Germanus promised their monastery in Bethlehem they would come back soon from Egypt. They stayed seven years. Abba Joseph taught them that it is often better to break a rash promise than keep it; they went back later, made peace with their elders, and returned to the desert.

Abbot Paul lived seven days' journey from any town, so his palm-leaf baskets could never be sold. He made them anyway, a daily quota all year, and each year burned the whole pile, to show that a monk cannot stay the course without work.

Patermucius entered a monastery with his eight-year-old son. To test him, the superior had the boy neglected and struck, then told the father to throw him in the river. He carried the child to the bank and threw him in; monks posted in advance pulled the boy out. Cassian tells it as a model of obedience.

The old monk Heron, fifty years in the desert, refused to break his fast even on Easter. At last he believed an angel's voice and threw himself down a well, sure he would be kept safe, and died. Cassian uses him to show that zeal without discretion destroys.

When the bishop of Alexandria taught that God has no body, most Egyptian monks were furious. The old monk Serapion was persuaded, but during prayer he burst into tears and cried out, 'They have taken away my God from me, and I have now none to lay hold of.'

Theonas, married five years, heard a sermon and begged his wife to join him in renouncing the world. She refused, and he left her for a monastery, saying 'it is safer for me to be divorced from a human person than from God.' Cassian tells the story, then insists he is not recommending that anyone leave a spouse.
After Chrysostom's first deposition, Cassian (then a deacon of Constantinople) and the priest Germanus carried the letter of Chrysostom's clergy to Pope Innocent in Rome.
stories.source: Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom, chapter 3

temperament.evidence: 'we recollect that when we were living in solitude a feeling of irritation would creep over us against our pen because it was too large or too small; against our penknife when it cut badly'

He passes on the old maxim that a monk should flee women and bishops, 'though I cannot produce it without shame on my own part, since I could not avoid my own sister, nor escape the hands of the bishop'.

temperament.trait: A bookish mind he could not switch off
temperament.evidence: He confessed to Abbot Nesteros that the poems and battle stories of his schooling came back to him even while he sang the psalms.
Of Germanus: 'everybody would say that a single heart and soul existed in our two bodies'.
His great theme is discretion: 'discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator.'

genuine_lines.quote: a monk who works is attacked by but one devil; but an idler is tormented by countless spirits.
genuine_lines.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For excess of fasting and gluttony come to the same thing
genuine_lines.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: It makes no difference whether gold plates, or lead, or what metal you please, are placed over our eyelids, the value of the metal makes no difference in our blindness.
genuine_lines.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered
genuine_lines.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: The opportunity for fasting is always with me. But as I am going to conduct you on your way, I cannot always keep you with me.
genuine_lines.work: Institutes, Book 5 (an Egyptian elder to Cassian and Germanus)
genuine_lines.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: O God, make speed to save me: O Lord, make haste to help me.
genuine_lines.work: Conferences, Conference 10 (Abbot Isaac, the prayer to be repeated always)
genuine_lines.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: A monk who works is attacked by one devil; an idle monk by a legion.
misattributed.truth: Genuine in Cassian, but he gives it as a saying 'handed down from the old fathers in Egypt', not as his own coinage (Institutes 10.23).

misattributed.line: Littera gesta docet, quid credas allegoria, moralis quid agas, quo tendas anagogia (the letter teaches what happened, allegory what to believe...).
misattributed.truth: A medieval rhyme (usually credited to Augustine of Dacia, 13th century), often hung on Cassian. Cassian's own passage is the 'one and the same Jerusalem' in four senses, Conference 14, chapter 8.
A label, not his word: 'Semipelagian' was coined more than a thousand years later. He wrote against Pelagius; his view that a good will can sometimes begin in us was attacked by Prosper of Aquitaine.

misattributed.line: Lines spoken by Abba Moses, Isaac, Joseph, Nesteros or Chaeremon, quoted as 'Cassian said'.
misattributed.truth: The Conferences are written by Cassian as talks with named Egyptian abbots. They are his teaching and he endorses them, but a careful quotation says 'Abba Joseph, in Cassian's Conferences'.

opinions.position: There is no such thing as justified anger at another person. The words 'without a cause' in 'whoever is angry with his brother' were added by people who wanted to keep their anger.
opinions.side_note: The strict side: all anger at others is forbidden, even 'righteous' anger. A clear contrast with Fathers who allow just anger.
opinions.quote: the words without a cause are superfluous, and were added by those who did not think that anger for just causes was to be banished
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split. Most people today think anger at injustice is healthy and even a duty; a minority, Christian and Buddhist alike, think all anger clouds judgment. Excellent statement.

opinions.topic: new: the one good use of anger
opinions.position: The only right use of anger is to turn it on your own sins and bad desires, never on other people.
opinions.quote: We have, it must be admitted, a use for anger excellently implanted in us for which alone it is useful and profitable for us to admit it, viz., when we are indignant and rage against the lustful emotions of our heart
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many people today think being hard on yourself is unhealthy; others think self-anger at your faults is how you change.

opinions.position: Going off alone does not make you patient. If you have not learned patience among people, your temper will find a pen or a flint to rage at. Solitude is for those already formed in community.
opinions.side_note: The 'community first' side: solitude is not an escape from your faults.
opinions.quote: Wherefore for a method of perfection it will not be of any use for there to be a dearth of men against whom our anger might be roused
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'I'm calmer when I'm alone, people are the problem' versus 'solitude just hides your problems'. Very recognisable today.

opinions.position: A monk should run from bishops (who will ordain him and pull him into public life) as from women. Office ruins the quiet of prayer.
opinions.side_note: The 'flee office' side, with a wry admission that he himself failed to avoid being ordained.
opinions.quote: Wherefore this is an old maxim of the Fathers that is still current — though I cannot produce it without shame on my own part, since I could not avoid my own sister, nor escape the hands of the bishop — viz., that a monk ought by all means to fly from women and bishops.
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: In modern form ('turn down promotions and positions of influence to keep your peace') it splits people well.

opinions.position: A lie is like a strong poison used as medicine: deadly if taken casually, but right to use when a great danger threatens, as the holy people of Scripture sometimes did.
opinions.side_note: The permissive side, taught by Abba Joseph in Cassian's Conferences and adopted by Cassian. Opposite to Augustine, who allowed no lies.
opinions.quote: And so we ought to regard a lie and to employ it as if its nature were that of hellebore; which is useful if taken when some deadly disease is threatening, but if taken without being required by some great danger is the cause of immediate death.
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree a lie can be right to save a life (the classic 'hiding someone from a murderer' case); a strict minority say never. Split, leaning his way.

opinions.position: If you made a rash promise and later see a better path, breaking it is not inconsistency; it is correcting a mistake.
opinions.side_note: He lived it: he and Germanus broke their promise to return to Bethlehem, staying seven years in Egypt.
opinions.quote: nor need we take it as a failure in consistency, but as a correction of rashness, whenever a promise that was faulty is corrected.
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Genuinely split: 'a promise is a promise' versus 'you shouldn't keep a promise that turned out to be a mistake'. A strong everyday statement.

opinions.position: God's grace comes first and does the most, but sometimes the first small step of good will comes from us; God sees it and strengthens it at once. Grace and free will work together.
opinions.side_note: The middle position between Augustine and Pelagius. Spoken by Abba Chaeremon in Conference 13; this is the chapter Prosper of Aquitaine attacked.
opinions.quote: And when He sees in us some beginnings of a good will, He at once enlightens it and strengthens it and urges it on towards salvation, increasing that which He Himself implanted or which He sees to have arisen from our own efforts.
opinions.work: Conferences, Conference 13 (Abbot Chaeremon, on the protection of God)
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most ordinary Christians today hold roughly this view without knowing it was ever controversial; Reformed Christians reject it. Split mainly among believers.

opinions.position: Scripture has four senses at once: the plain history, the meaning about the Church, the meaning about heaven, and the moral meaning for your own soul.
opinions.side_note: The layered-meaning side, taught by Abba Nesteros.
opinions.quote: so that one and the same Jerusalem can be taken in four senses: historically as the city of the Jews; allegorically as Church of Christ, anagogically as the heavenly city of God which is the mother of us all, tropologically, as the soul of man
opinions.work: Conferences, Conference 14 (Abbot Nesteros, on spiritual knowledge)
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split between readers who look for hidden spiritual meanings and those who want only what the author meant. A good statement if phrased plainly.

opinions.position: His classical schooling was a burden: the poems and war stories he learned as a boy crowded into his prayers. Fill the mind with Scripture instead.
opinions.side_note: His own confession, answered by Abba Nesteros. The wary side on secular learning.
opinions.quote: my mind is filled with those songs of the poets so that even at the hour of prayer it is thinking about those trifling fables, and the stories of battles with which from its earliest infancy it was stored by its childish lessons
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: In modern form ('what you watch and read as a child stays in your head and shapes your prayers and thoughts; be careful what goes in') it splits people.

opinions.position: Extremes meet. Fasting too hard does as much harm as gluttony, and endless vigils as much as sleeping too much. Discretion, not intensity, is the chief virtue.
opinions.side_note: The moderate side of asceticism.
opinions.quote: For excess of fasting and gluttony come to the same thing, and an unlimited continuance of vigils is equally injurious to a monk as the torpor of a deep sleep
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree with moderation; the split is with people who admire going all-in (extreme fasting, extreme training).

opinions.topic: new: kindness over your own rules
opinions.position: When a guest comes, break your fast and eat with them. You can fast any time; you cannot keep the guest. Love of neighbour outranks your private discipline.
opinions.side_note: Said by an Egyptian elder and presented by Cassian as the example to follow.
opinions.quote: And a fast, although it is useful and advisable, is yet a free-will offering. But the exigencies of a command require the fulfilment of a work of charity.
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split in everyday form: 'I'd break my diet (or my routine, or my Lent) to eat with a friend' versus 'I keep my commitments whatever the company'.

opinions.position: Idleness is the soul's greatest danger. A monk must work with his hands every day, even if the work has no use, as Abbot Paul burned his baskets every year.
opinions.side_note: He gives the saying as the Egyptian fathers'.
opinions.quote: a monk who works is attacked by but one devil; but an idler is tormented by countless spirits.
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'idle hands are the devil's workshop' versus 'rest and doing nothing are good for you'. Works well.

opinions.topic: new: telling someone your dark thoughts
opinions.position: Tell an experienced elder every tempting or troubling thought. A bad thought loses its power the moment it is brought into the open.
opinions.side_note: Taught by Abba Moses; the root of later spiritual direction.
opinions.quote: For a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many people (and therapists) agree that speaking a thought aloud weakens it; many others keep their inner life private. A good statement.

opinions.position: Obedience to your spiritual superior can outrank even love for your own child; he holds up a father who was ready to throw his son in the river at the abbot's word.
opinions.side_note: He tells it as praise. Separately, he tells of Theonas leaving his unwilling wife but refuses to endorse it (Conference 21, chapter 10).
opinions.quote: Then he, as if this had been commanded him by the Lord, at once snatched up the child as quickly as possible, and carried him in his arms to the river's bank to throw him in.
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: One-sided today: almost everyone would be horrified. Useful only as a 'sparring partner' reveal, not as a statement.

opinions.position: The only friendship that lasts is between people alike in goodness. Friendships built on usefulness, shared interests or family ties break when circumstances change.
opinions.side_note: Taught by Abba Joseph. Cassian's own lifelong friendship with Germanus is the example.
opinions.quote: there is one kind of love which is indissoluble, where the union is owing not to the favour of a recommendation, or some great kindness or gifts, or the reason of some bargain, or the necessities of nature, but simply to similarity of virtue.
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many think friends can differ widely in values and still be close; others think deep friendship needs shared values.

opinions.position: A humble person is not quick to laugh. Readiness to laugh is a sign that humility is missing.
opinions.side_note: The austere side; it is one of ten signs of humility given by Abbot Pinufius.
opinions.quote: tenthly, if he is not easily moved or too ready to laugh. For by such signs and the like is true humility recognised.
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Mostly against him today; laughter is widely seen as healthy and humble. A sparring statement.

opinions.topic: new: one short prayer all day
opinions.position: Pray one short verse over and over, in every mood and task, until it fills the mind: 'O God, make speed to save me: O Lord, make haste to help me.'
opinions.side_note: Taught by Abba Isaac; this verse became the opening of every service in the Western daily office.
opinions.quote: And so for keeping up continual recollection of God this pious formula is to be ever set before you. O God, make speed to save me: O Lord, make haste to help me
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split among praying people: short repeated prayers versus prayer in your own spontaneous words (many evangelicals distrust repetition).

sparring.over: Grace and free will. Prosper's Against the Conferencer (c. 433) attacked Conference 13 without naming Cassian, while granting him unusual virtue.

Whether Mary is Mother of God and how Christ is one. At the request of the Roman archdeacon Leo (later Pope Leo I) he wrote On the Incarnation of the Lord (430) against Nestorius, blaming Pelagianism as the root.
sparring.source: On the Incarnation of the Lord, against Nestorius; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'John Cassian'

sparring.over: Whether God has a human-like body. He sided with Bishop Theophilus's letter against the many monks who were enraged by it.

portraits.title: Saint John Cassian, miniature in the Sacra Parallela of John of Damascus (BnF, Grec 923, f. 74v)
St John Cassian the Roman, Russian icon (centre panel)
St John Cassian the Roman, Russian icon with border scenes

figures.name: Pelagius
figures.dates: c. 354-360 to after 418 (last heard of about 418)
figures.places: Born in Britain (his opponents call him a Briton; Jerome's jibe about 'Scots' porridge' has suggested an Irish link); Rome (c. 380s to 410), a teacher to Christian noble families; fled the Gothic sack of Rome to Sicily and North Africa (410-411); Palestine (411-c. 418); afterwards unknown, perhaps Egypt
figures.role: Lay monk, spiritual adviser and Bible commentator; the moral reformer whose name became a heresy
figures.status_note: Condemned as a heretic. Acquitted by fourteen bishops at the Synod of Diospolis (Lydda, 415) after disowning several propositions; then condemned by African councils (Carthage and Milevis, 416; Carthage, 418), by Pope Innocent I (417) and Pope Zosimus (418, after first favouring him), and banished from Rome by imperial decree (418). The Council of Ephesus (431) condemned his cause. Not a saint anywhere. Caution: most of his own writings survived only under Jerome's name or in the quotations of his opponents (chiefly Augustine), and many texts called 'Pelagian' were written by his followers, not by him.
figures.hook: When a bishop in Rome quoted Augustine's prayer 'Give what You command, and command what You will', Pelagius could not bear it and nearly started a quarrel on the spot; he thought it let Christians off the hook.

stories.story: In Rome someone quoted Augustine's prayer from the Confessions, 'Give what You command, and command what You will.' Pelagius, Augustine heard, 'could not bear' the words and argued so excitedly that he nearly came to a quarrel with the bishop who quoted them.
stories.source: Augustine, On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 53 [20]

stories.story: At the Synod of Diospolis (415) fourteen Palestinian bishops questioned him on charges sent from the West. He affirmed that a person can be without sin if he wishes, by the capacity God gave, disowned the rest ('The rest were not said by me'), anathematized them, and was declared a catholic. Augustine argued that the acquittal condemned the doctrines even while it cleared the man.
stories.source: Augustine, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, chapters 6 and 24

stories.story: In 413 the young Roman noblewoman Demetrias, heir of the richest family in Rome, refused her arranged marriage and took the veil. Her mother asked Pelagius, Jerome and Augustine to write to her; Pelagius's letter opens by praising what human nature can do. It survived for centuries under Jerome's name.
stories.source: Letter to Demetrias, chapters 1-2; Schaff, History of the Christian Church vol. 3, section 147

stories.story: Augustine first met his writings (brief notes on Paul's letters) as those of 'a holy man, as I am told, who has made no small progress in the Christian life', and answered his argument against inherited sin without naming him as a heretic.
stories.source: Augustine, On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, Book 3, chapter 1

stories.story: At a synod in Jerusalem in 415 the Spanish priest Orosius reported Augustine's charges; Pelagius is said to have answered, 'And who is Augustine to me?'
stories.source: Orosius, Liber Apologeticus (reported in secondary sources; not read in the original here)

temperament.trait: Earnest moral reformer, respected for his life
temperament.evidence: Augustine, before the controversy: 'a holy man, as I am told, who has made no small progress in the Christian life'.
temperament.source: Augustine, On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, Book 3, chapter 1

temperament.trait: Easily roused when he thought faith was being made an excuse
temperament.evidence: On Augustine's prayer 'Give what You command': he 'could not bear; and contradicting somewhat too excitedly, nearly came to a quarrel with him who had mentioned them.'
temperament.source: Augustine, On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 53

temperament.evidence: At Diospolis he distanced himself from his disciple Caelestius's sharper statements: 'The rest were not said by me... I do not feel that I am responsible.'
temperament.source: Augustine, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, chapter 24

temperament.trait: A motivator who starts from hope
temperament.evidence: His stated habit is first to show people what human nature can do, because 'every longing after anything dies within us, so soon as we despair of attaining that thing.'
temperament.source: Letter to Demetrias, chapter 2 (in Schaff's translation)

genuine_lines.quote: For his willing, therefore, and doing a good work, the praise belongs to man; or rather both to man, and to God who has bestowed on him the 'capacity' for his will and work, and who evermore by the help of His grace assists even this capacity.
genuine_lines.work: In Defence of Free Will, Book 1, quoted by Augustine in On the Grace of Christ, Book 1
genuine_lines.translation: P. Holmes and R. E. Wallis, rev. B. B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5 (1887), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: I once more repeat my position: I say that it is possible for a man to be without sin.
genuine_lines.work: On Nature, quoted by Augustine in On Nature and Grace
genuine_lines.translation: P. Holmes and R. E. Wallis, rev. B. B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5 (1887), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: we are procreated as without virtue, so also without vice
genuine_lines.work: In Defence of Free Will, Book 1, quoted by Augustine in On Original Sin
genuine_lines.translation: P. Holmes and R. E. Wallis, rev. B. B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5 (1887), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: As often as I have to speak concerning moral improvement and the leading of a holy life, I am accustomed first to set forth the power and quality of human nature, and to show what it can accomplish.
genuine_lines.translation: P. Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3 (1867; 5th ed. 1884)

genuine_lines.quote: It is hard, it is steep, we cannot; we are only human, wrapped in frail flesh. O blind madness! O profane rashness!
genuine_lines.original_text: Durum est, arduum est, non possumus; homines sumus, fragili carne circumdamur. O caecam insaniam! o profanam temeritatem!
genuine_lines.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30; also printed in B. J. Kidd, Documents Illustrative of the History of the Church, vol. 2, 1923)

genuine_lines.quote: I conquer the greatest things, and am conquered by the small.
genuine_lines.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30)

misattributed.line: Take away the rich and you will find no poor (Tolle divitem et pauperem non invenies).
misattributed.truth: From the treatise On Riches (De divitiis) by an anonymous follower (often called 'the Sicilian Briton'), not by Pelagius. At Diospolis Pelagius disowned the proposition that the baptized rich cannot enter the kingdom unless they give up everything (Augustine, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, chapters 23-24).

A modern summary of his view (and a slogan of Kant's ethics: 'ought implies can'), not a sentence in his writings. His real lines are about God commanding nothing impossible (Letter to Demetrias, chapter 16).
A later guess (Welsh 'Morgan', sea-born, as if translated into Greek 'Pelagius'), with no ancient evidence.

misattributed.line: The Letter to Demetrias and the Commentary on Paul's Letters as works of Jerome.
misattributed.truth: Both are by Pelagius; they survived for centuries among Jerome's works (Schaff, History of the Christian Church vol. 3, section 147).

misattributed.line: Sayings of Caelestius or Julian of Eclanum (for example 'Adam's sin injured himself alone') quoted as Pelagius's.
misattributed.truth: These are his followers' sharper formulations. Pelagius disowned several of them at Diospolis, though Augustine argued he held the same views.

opinions.position: God gives us the ability to do good; wanting to and actually doing it are up to us, so the praise for a good life belongs to the person (and to God who gave the ability and helps it).
opinions.side_note: The 'effort' pole in its clearest form. Condemned by the Church; Augustine held the opposite.
opinions.quote: For his willing, therefore, and doing a good work, the praise belongs to man; or rather both to man, and to God who has bestowed on him the 'capacity' for his will and work, and who evermore by the help of His grace assists even this capacity.
opinions.work: In Defence of Free Will, Book 1, quoted by Augustine in On the Grace of Christ, Book 1
opinions.translation: P. Holmes and R. E. Wallis, rev. B. B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5 (1887), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split. Many people, Christian or not, believe you earn credit for being good; Reformed and many other Christians say every good in us is God's gift. Excellent statement in plain words ('the credit for a good life belongs mostly to the person who lived it').

opinions.position: Babies are born neither good nor bad. Everything we are praised or blamed for is something we do, not something we are born with.
opinions.side_note: Denies inherited guilt from Adam (original sin), the heart of the Augustinian case against him.
opinions.quote: Everything good, and everything evil, on account of which we are either laudable or blameworthy, is not born with us but done by us: for we are born not fully developed, but with a capacity for either conduct; and we are procreated as without virtue, so also without vice
opinions.work: In Defence of Free Will, Book 1, quoted by Augustine in On Original Sin
opinions.translation: P. Holmes and R. E. Wallis, rev. B. B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5 (1887), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split. Most people outside the churches, and many inside, think babies are born innocent; traditional Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teaching says otherwise. Very strong statement.

opinions.topic: new: can anyone live without sinning
opinions.position: It is possible for a person to live without sin. He does not claim anyone has done it from infancy, only that it can be done, and that a converted sinner can stop sinning.
opinions.side_note: At Diospolis he added: 'by his own labour and God's grace'.
opinions.quote: I once more repeat my position: I say that it is possible for a man to be without sin. What do you say? That it is impossible for a man to be without sin?
opinions.work: On Nature, quoted by Augustine in On Nature and Grace
opinions.translation: P. Holmes and R. E. Wallis, rev. B. B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5 (1887), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: One-sided against him among most Christians ('nobody's perfect'); some holiness traditions and many non-Christians who think people can be fully good would lean his way. Works as a sparring statement.

opinions.position: Scripture shows people who lived without sin, men and women alike, and above all the mother of the Lord, whose piety had no sin in it.
opinions.side_note: Augustine agreed about Mary alone, 'out of honour to the Lord'. Reported in Augustine's words with Pelagius's phrase quoted.
opinions.quote: for of her, he says, we must needs allow that her piety had no sin in it.
opinions.work: On Nature, reported by Augustine in On Nature and Grace
opinions.translation: P. Holmes and R. E. Wallis, rev. B. B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5 (1887), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split along church lines: Catholics and Orthodox say Mary was sinless; most Protestants say only Christ was. Few today would say Abel or Daniel never sinned.

opinions.position: Good people exist outside the faith. Many pagan philosophers were chaste, patient, generous and just, which shows the goodness God built into human nature.
opinions.side_note: Uses good pagans as proof of nature's goodness. Opposite to Augustine's view that pagan virtues were splendid vices.
opinions.quote: How many philosophers have we heard of, read of, and seen for ourselves, chaste, patient, modest, generous, self-controlled, kind, spurning the world's honours and its pleasures alike, lovers of justice no less than of knowledge!
opinions.original_text: Quam multos enim philosophorum et audivimus et legimus, et ipsi vidimus castos, patientes, modestos, liberales, abstinentes, benignos, et honores mundi simul, et delicias respuentes, et amatores justitiae non minus quam scientiae
opinions.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30)
opinions.today: Most people today agree that non-believers can be truly good; some Christians hold that no one is good apart from God. Leans his way, still splits believers.

opinions.topic: new: the freedom to do wrong
opinions.position: Being able to choose evil is itself a good thing, because it makes our goodness our own choice. God could have made us unable to sin, but then our goodness would not be ours.
opinions.quote: this very fact, that we are also able to do evil, is good
opinions.original_text: hoc quoque ipsum quod etiam mala facere possumus, bonum est
opinions.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30)
opinions.today: Split: many think free will is worth the evil it allows; others think a world where no one could do harm would be better. Strong statement.

opinions.position: Everyone has a built-in sense of right and wrong. We blush or go pale at wrongdoing and want our good deeds known: that is nature's own holiness judging inside us.
opinions.quote: For there is, I say, in our souls a certain natural holiness, so to speak
opinions.original_text: Est enim, inquam, in animis nostris naturalis quaedam (ut ita dixerim) sanctitas
opinions.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30)
opinions.today: Split: many believe in an inborn moral sense; others think conscience is learned from upbringing and culture.

opinions.position: Saying 'it's too hard, I'm only human' is an insult to God, as if He did not know what He made or commanded the impossible and then punished us for it.
opinions.side_note: His central complaint against lax Christians.
opinions.quote: It is hard, it is steep, we cannot; we are only human, wrapped in frail flesh. O blind madness! O profane rashness!
opinions.original_text: Durum est, arduum est, non possumus; homines sumus, fragili carne circumdamur. O caecam insaniam! o profanam temeritatem!
opinions.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30)
opinions.today: Strongly split, and very everyday: 'I'm only human' is a common and accepted excuse; many others hate it as a cop-out. Excellent statement.

opinions.position: You cannot pick and choose which of God's commands to keep. None is a small matter, because of Who gave it.
opinions.quote: For we must not choose some of God's commands as if at our own discretion, but fulfil them all without exception; nor despise any of His precepts as cheap and little trifles
opinions.original_text: Non enim quasi ad arbitrium nostrum quaedam ex mandatis Dei debemus eligere, sed generaliter universa complere; nec aliqua praecepta ejus quasi vilia munuscula ac parva contemnere
opinions.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30)
opinions.today: Split: many believers treat some rules as minor or cultural; others say all of it binds. A good statement ('there is no such thing as a small sin').

opinions.position: People who manage heroic fasting and self-denial then give in to easy, everyday faults like envy and temper. If you can do the hard things, you have no excuse for the small ones.
opinions.side_note: Spoken in the voice of the inconsistent person he is mocking.
opinions.quote: I tackle hard and toilsome things without a worry, and I believe the easier ones cannot be done. I conquer the greatest things, and am conquered by the small.
opinions.original_text: Res difficiles et laboris plenas securus aggredior, et faciliora non posse fieri credo. Vinco maxima, vincendus a parvis.
opinions.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30)
opinions.today: Recognisable to many; less a split than a mirror. Could become 'the big sacrifices are easier for me than the small daily kindnesses'.

opinions.position: Never run anyone down, and do not even believe those who do. Putting others down to look better is the mark of small people.
opinions.quote: It is not enough to say that you must not slander; you must never even believe a slanderer.
opinions.original_text: Parum diximus, non solum ipsa non detrahas, sed ne detrahenti quidem aliquando credas.
opinions.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30)
opinions.today: Split in practice: most say gossip is wrong, but many think it is fine to listen, or that talking about people is normal and harmless.

opinions.position: Remember your noble birth only as a standard to beat: outdo your family's fame with the holiness of your life.
opinions.side_note: Written to the heiress of Rome's greatest family.
opinions.quote: Remember your nobility only for this: to rival the lustre of your family with holiness of life.
opinions.original_text: Nobilitatis ad hoc tantum memineris, ut cum claritate generis, morum sanctitate contendas
opinions.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30)
opinions.today: Mostly agreed in principle; weak as a statement unless recast ('your family's name should push you to do better').

opinions.position: Chastity is not the whole of holiness. A virgin who hates, envies, grasps or rages is not holy in spirit; a person can sin in any part of goodness.
opinions.side_note: Against treating sexual purity as the measure of a good Christian.
opinions.quote: She who is holy in body and spirit does wrong neither in her limbs nor in her mind. And one can do wrong not only in the matter of chastity, but in any part of righteousness.
opinions.original_text: Quae corpore et spiritu sancta est, nec in membris, nec in mente delinquit. Delinquere autem non in causa castitatis tantum esse potest, sed etiam in quacumque parte justitiae.
opinions.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 30)
opinions.today: Most people agree; it splits only those who treat sexual sin as the gravest kind. Could be phrased as 'a bad temper is as serious as a sexual sin'.

opinions.topic: new: start from what you can do
opinions.position: Teach goodness by first showing people what human nature can achieve. Hope is what gets anyone started; nobody tries for what they think impossible.
opinions.quote: As often as I have to speak concerning moral improvement and the leading of a holy life, I am accustomed first to set forth the power and quality of human nature, and to show what it can accomplish.
opinions.translation: P. Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3 (1867; 5th ed. 1884)
opinions.today: Split: 'people change when you believe in them' versus 'people change when they face how weak they are'. A good statement about how to help someone change.

sparring.over: Grace, free will, original sin and whether anyone can live without sin. Augustine wrote On Nature and Grace (415), On the Proceedings of Pelagius (417) and On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin (418) against him.
sparring.source: Augustine, On Nature and Grace; On the Proceedings of Pelagius; On the Grace of Christ

sparring.over: Whether a person can be without sin and free of passions. Jerome attacked him in the Letter to Ctesiphon (133) and the Dialogue against the Pelagians (415), and elsewhere mocked him as 'stuffed with Scots' porridge' (prologue to his Commentary on Jeremiah; read here only in secondary sources).
sparring.source: Jerome, Letter 133; Dialogue against the Pelagians

sparring.over: Carried Augustine's charges to the synod of Jerusalem (415) and wrote a Defence (Liber Apologeticus) against him.
First inclined to clear him, then, after the African bishops protested, condemned him in the circular letter (Tractoria) of 418.
